The late Harappan cultures are primarily Chalcolithic in which tools of stone and copper are used. 5. II. They do not show metal objects requiring complicated casting. III. The Chalcolithic people in the later Harappan phase lived in villages. IV. In the late Harappan phase at Bhagwanpura in Haryana, burnt bricks were not found.
x: Late Harappan cultures represent the final phase of the Indus Valley Civilization after the decline of its urban centers around 1900 BCE. These cultures were largely Chalcolithic, meaning people used both stone and copper tools. The settlements became smaller and mostly rural villages, reflecting the collapse of urban planning and centralized authority. These societies lacked advanced metallurgical techniques such as complex casting. Archaeological evidence from sites like Bhagwanpura (Haryana) shows continuation of Harappan traditions including the use of burnt bricks, but with reduced urban sophistication. Therefore statements I, II and III are correct.

s: In which Veda are Sabha and Samiti declared as separate institutions?
x: Among the Vedic texts, Sabha and Samiti are clearly mentioned as separate institutions in the Atharvaveda, although both these institutions (Sabha and Samiti) are also mentioned in the Rigveda. s: Rig-vedic religion was–
x: The most interesting aspect of Rig Vedic religion was its polytheistic character in which a number of Gods were worshipped. Other than this in Rigveda Ekeshwarvaad is supported by saying Ekam Satt Vipra bahudha badanti". Ekeshwarvaad of Rigveda included vision of Advaityavaad, Sarvadevtavaad and Bahudevatavaad.
